title: Soccer Goal Nets Came Out of a Fight Over Whether It Was a Goal
hook: Before nets, a team could score and be told the ball never went in

open.title: In old soccer, you could score and be told you hadn't
open.line: A soccer ground in Liverpool, England, 1889. A ball that clearly seemed to go in, and the referee waved it off. The crowd booed.

summary: After a goal dispute in 1889, Liverpool engineer John Brodie patented a net to hang behind the goal. He later named it his proudest invention.

text: Soccer goals in the 1880s had no nets.
A ball between the posts just rolled on behind.
An Everton kick from almost level with the post drew cheers.
The referee said it never went between the posts.
The crowd booed, and it ended 2 to 2.

panels.text: With a net, we'd know right away!

text: Civil engineer John Brodie was reportedly in the crowd.
Papers printed letters blaming the referee's eyes.
Brodie thought of a pouch behind the goal to catch balls.
He chose netting, not boards or cloth, so fans could see.
Actually, the first design had a bell.
It rang when the ball hit the net.
He applied for a patent on November 28, 1889, a month later.
From November 1891, every English league match had nets.
He later helped design the Mersey road tunnel.
Yet he named the net his proudest invention.

sources: Everton Heritage Society: Net Gains, John Alexander Brodie’s Sporting and Civic Legacy
